av_event.line_text: Mine's going to be doing my fuses for free. He just doesn't know it yet.
av_event.what: A teenage boy in a hoodie walks across the kitchen behind Karen, opens the fridge on the right, takes out a carton of milk, and walks back out of frame without looking at the camera.

text:
B: Hello. Can you hear me alright?
A: Er, yeah, yeah. Loud and clear. Hi. I'm Andrew.
B: Karen. So we've just got to chat, have we?
A: Seems that way, yeah. Three minutes. Erm, I'm not sure there's a topic, I suppose.
B: No. Did you finish that puzzle thing at the start?
A: Er, most of it. I got stuck on the last one, the one with the shapes. I sort of ran out of time just staring at it.
B: Same. I hate leaving things half done. I do Wordle every morning and if I don't get it, it bothers me all day.
A: What's your streak?
B: Two hundred and twelve.
A: That's, er, that's quite serious.
B: It is serious. So what do you do?
A: Erm, well, I'm a GIS analyst. For a water company, in Nottingham. So it's mapping, basically. Where all the pipes are, which bits flood, that sort of thing. People come to me when a dataset doesn't make sense, and I sort it out. Mostly from a back bedroom, as you can probably see.
B: I did wonder about the bike on the wall.
A: Yeah. It lives there. Kate, my wife, wouldn't have it in the hall.
B: Fair enough. I'd be the same. My son leaves his stuff all over the hallway and it drives me mad.
A: How old is he?
B: Seventeen. Doing an electrical apprenticeship. So there's tools and boots and a college bag, every single night, right where you walk in.
A: Useful though, an electrician. My dad was one. He still does all his own wiring, which my mum's not keen on.
B: Mine's going to be doing my fuses for free. He just doesn't know it yet.
A: And what about you, what's your job?
B: Office and transport admin at a haulage firm near Gatwick. Timesheets, MOTs, service schedules, purchase orders. Basically anything the managers don't want comes to me. Drivers are the worst. You ask for timesheets by Friday and you get them the following Wednesday, screwed up in a ball, with tea on them.
A: Sounds like some of the data I get, to be honest.
B: Does it?
A: Er, yeah. Contractors fill in a form, they put the pipe size in the wrong field, or the coordinates are in the sea off Skegness. And then I'm the one who has to sort of work out what they meant.
B: Yeah. And nobody thanks you for it, because when it's right nobody notices.
A: That's it, really. That's exactly it.
B: I keep saying I want "office manager" on my contract, since that's what I actually do.
A: You should, I suppose. I'm the opposite. I'd quite like to never manage anybody.
B: Can't blame you. Half of them can't manage themselves.
A: Yeah. Er, are you local to Gatwick, then?
B: Crawley. Born and bred. Ten minutes from work if the A23's behaving, which it never is.
A: We've got tram works in Beeston at the minute, so I sympathise. Everything's coned off for about a mile.
B: Is that near where—
